newsitem.title: USA: US chip industry book-to-bill seen up in August.
newsitem.headline: US chip industry book-to-bill seen up in August.

text.p: The U.S. semiconductor market may finally provide a solid reason for optimism next week, with analysts predicting improvement in the latest book-to-bill ratio -- a widely watched measure of computer chip demand.
Analysts' forecasts for the August book-to-bill ratio range from 0.86 to 0.92, with all of those polled predicting that orders inched higher. July's book to bill ratio was 0.85.
"We've seen a prolonged correction in bookings (orders). We think that is over," said Charles Boucher of UBS Securities.
The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association expects to release the industry's book-to-bill report on Monday.
The ratio measures new chip orders against sales in a month. July's 0.85 ratio, for example, meant $85 worth of orders came in for every $100 in chips sold that month.
Analysts said orders appeared to pick up in August from July, especially for various chips used in personal computers.
Dan Niles of Robertson, Stephens & Co has predicted a substantial increase in the ratio to 0.92.
"August rolls around, and people start building up parts for big PC shipments in September," he said.
Bear Stearns analyst Nimal Vallipuram also said increased demand from personal computer makers would push the ratio higher, although his estimate is a more conservative 0.86.
"But that doesn't mean August was a good month," Vallipuram cautioned.
Indeed, a ratio below one - whether it is 0.86 or 0.92 - means that orders are below sales, indicating the future is not as bright as the past.
Analysts said they expected orders in September to show even greater improvement than in August, which is traditionally a slow month.

August is usually the weakest month of the year for the semiconductor business because many manufacturers shut down for vacation. Thus, an increase in orders during August could signal the beginning of a cyclical upturn.

National Semiconductor Corp on Thursday provided evidence that orders from PC makers started to rebound. Although the company reported a drop in earnings, it told analysts that its orders last month were 30 percent higher than in July.

The last two weeks of September are when PC makers start shipping their products for the holiday season, and most of them order semiconductors "just-in-time," often only days before they are scheduled for the assembly line.

To be sure, analysts are still not optimistic about memory chips, a category in which prices continue to drop. Even as unit volumes strengthen, continual price declines push total orders lower than in the previous month, they said,
Micron Technology Inc and Texas Instruments Inc are the two big U.S. memory chip makers. The other major memory chip makers are in Japan, Korea and Taiwan.
